text.p: Following are the main stories in Croatian newspapers on Wednesday.
VJESNIK
- A group of Serbs assaulted Croatian officials handing out pensions in the last Serb-held enclave, stoning their bus and smashing windows of their mobile office.
- Croatia is seeking favourable loans for financing imports of 50-60,000 tonnes of wheat and 20,000 tonnes of sunflower oil from the United States. Americans offered good terms for soy imports.
- Croatia plans new policy on road construction and maintenance, state funds to be doubled next year, says Transport Minister Zeljko Luzavec.

- Women make up some eight percent in Croatian parliament. Some 68 percent of Zagreb citizens think women do not participate enough in public life and 72 percent are against abortion ban, according to a recently conducted poll,
- Statistical data show Zagreb is the safest town in Europe.
- Insolvent companies increased their debts by half a billion kuna in November to total 7.8 billion kuna, with private firms accounting for 4.6 billion kuna of the debts.
- The government is close to reaching a deal with the Hungarian oil company MOL for the sale of 12.5 percent in the Adritic crude pipeline operator Janaf for 92.8 million German marks.
VECERNJI LIST
- Serb leaders from the enclave of Eastern Slavonia recommended to local Serbs to accept Croatian citizenship.
- Textile firm Varteks may loose the licence for manufacturing Levi's jeans unless it is fully privatised.

- Government holdings in Croatian companies have shrunk to 18 billion kuna in the past year from 30 billion mostly through distribution of shares packages for various purposes, including rehabilitation of troubled companies, financing of construction works.
- Commentary by V. Sonje: A strong rise in 1996 imports was for the most part spurred by increased investment activity.
- Lawyers make the best tax advisers, says president of the bar association M. Hanzekovic in an interview.
SLOBODNA DALMACIJA

- Italians who left Croatia after World War II are now demanding the return of their property. Croatia is offering to pay the debt of $35 million either fully in cash or $17.6 million in cash and the rest in shares of Adriatic hotels.
- Two top meat processors say veterinary checks on meat imported from Germany showed no sign of any disease. Croatia recently banned imports of beef.
- Average net salaries totalled 2,124 kuna in November, up 2.6 percent from October. Highest salaries were paid by liquor and tobacco producers.
- December retail sales rose 12.2 percent from a month before, and 29.5 percent from December 1995.
- The number of overnights rose 67 percent to 21.5 million last year, with foreign tourists accounting for 16.6 million. -- Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075
